Short answer: I won't do the full derivation here, and for your makerspace assistant you shouldn't train a model at all. Your `MISSION.md` lists training and the math inside models as out of scope. A full PPO derivation also needs policy gradients, which come after some machine-learning background you haven't had yet.

Here is what RL means for tool use, using a game. Picture a bot in a game engine that picks an action, gets a score, and nudges itself toward actions that scored well. Tool calling works the same way. The model tries a tool call, such as booking the laser cutter. A reward then says whether it worked: the right slot, the right arguments, the booking confirmed. Training makes the rewarded calls more likely.

PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) is the safety rule on that nudging. It compares the new model's chance of making a call with the old model's chance. It then caps how far one update can move that ratio, so one lucky score can't wreck what the model already does well.

The premise to fix is "the best agents are trained with RL". That is true for the labs that build the base models. It isn't how teams like yours get a good agent. Training needs thousands of scored examples, GPUs and a lot of money, which your small sponsor budget can't cover. Your tool-calling quality will mostly come from clear tool descriptions, a sensible workflow and the right context. Those are in your mission, and they are cheap.

If you want, I can teach a short lesson on how tool calling is trained, or one on writing a good tool description for the booking tool.

Quick check: why would a model get better at booking from a clearer tool description, with no training?
